analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 16% and limits most credit card fees to $15.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 72 cosponsors but was referred to committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a 16% interest-rate ceiling into federal law for credit card accounts, counting annual and membership fees toward that ceiling so issuers could not get around it. It also would have capped late fees, overdraft fees, and over-the-limit fees at $15, and blocked credit card rate increases that happened between the bill's introduction and 60 days after enactment. The Federal Reserve could adjust the ceiling upward only if severe economic conditions justified it, and Congress could veto any increase.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit cardholders, especially those carrying balances at rates above 16%, would gain a legally enforceable ceiling on their interest rate, with annual and membership fees counted toward that ceiling so issuers could not simply re-label interest as fees [S2][S3]. Cardholders who incur late, overdraft, or over-the-limit fees would see those fees capped at $15 [S2][S3]. Cardholders whose accounts carried a rate under 16% as of December 11, 2009 would be protected from rate increases in the gap before the cap took effect [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cardholders paying high rates and fees

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit card accounts at 16%, applying both to new borrowing and to outstanding balances.
Counts annual fees, membership fees, and other account-opening charges toward the 16% APR cap, closing the common workaround of moving interest into fixed fees.
Caps late fees, overdraft fees, insufficient-funds fees, and over-the-limit fees at $15.

Treats any rate increase on accounts below 16% as of December 11, 2009, raised during the window before the cap took effect, as an unfair or deceptive act or practice, protecting existing cardholders from rate hikes in the interim.

Requires the Federal Reserve to justify any increase of the cap as presumed contrary to the public interest absent severe economic conditions, and gives Congress 90 days to veto an increase by joint resolution.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and the banks behind them would bear the cost: the 16% APR cap would cut interest revenue on cards now carrying higher rates, counting annual and membership fees toward the APR would prevent replacing lost interest with fixed fees [S2][S3], and the $15 cap would directly limit late, overdraft, and over-the-limit fee income [S2][S3]. Some of the cost could be passed back to borrowers through reduced access to credit, since issuers price higher rates to cover riskier customers [S2].

drawbacks.text: A strict 16% cap can price higher-risk borrowers out of credit entirely: issuers who can no longer charge rates that reflect a borrower's risk may decline to lend to them at all, so some people who today carry balances at 20% or more could lose access to card credit rather than get cheaper credit.

The $15 fee cap removes the fee income that funds rewards programs and no-annual-fee cards, so the cost of the cap could partly reappear as fewer perks, higher rates near the new ceiling, or tighter approval standards rather than pure savings for borrowers.
The cap applies to outstanding balances as well as new borrowing, an unusually retroactive feature that would hit issuer revenues sharply and could prompt cutbacks in credit lines elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households carrying credit card debt, the direct benefits are large and concrete: a hard 16% ceiling with fees counted toward it, and penalty fees cut to $15, would save real money for exactly the borrowers who pay the most today. The honest cost is that a hard national cap does not distinguish between borrowers, so lenders would likely respond by issuing fewer cards to people with poor credit, and the retroactive application to existing balances would squeeze issuers harder than a cap limited to new lending. The bill anticipated the classic fee-shifting workaround, which makes it better designed than most usury caps, but the access-to-credit tradeoff is real and falls on some of the same people the bill aims to help.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services and Rules Committees the day it was introduced and never moved again, dying quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 11, 2009 and referred the same day to the House Financial Services Committee and the House Rules Committee.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the action history ends with the day-one referrals.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 without the bill receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and the banks behind them are better off: no cap was ever enacted, so they kept charging interest rates above 16% and fees above $15 through the end of the Congress and beyond.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers, whose rates and fees stayed uncapped

for.name: Rep. John F. Tierney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 72 original cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: Chaired the House Financial Services Committee during the 111th Congress, under which the bill sat without a markup or hearing after referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; support as shown by cosponsorship was nearly all Democratic (70 of 253 House Democrats and 2 of 178 House Republicans).

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer banks
industries.note: The bill would cut directly into the two main profit engines of card lending: interest above 16% and penalty fees above $15. By counting annual and membership fees toward the APR cap, it also blocked the standard workaround of shifting cost onto fixed fees, and by treating rate increases during the enactment window as an unfair or deceptive practice it closed the door on raising rates ahead of the deadline.
